### Reviewer 4

The manuscript presents a clear and compelling strategy to suppress electron–phonon (EP) coupling in CsPbI₃
nanoplatelets (NPLs), which has long been a critical bottleneck limiting the spectral purity and device performance of pure-
red PeLEDs. The introduction of a rigid ligand—4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonamide (AEBS)—as a “rigid-ligand pinning”
motif is conceptually strong and addresses the fundamental issue of lattice softness and dynamic disorder originating from
long-chain oleylamine ligands. The authors convincingly demonstrate that AEBS anchoring suppresses lattice vibrations,
reduces EP coupling strength, and narrows both PL and EL linewidths.
Importantly, the achieved device metrics—an EL FWHM of 24 nm, a peak EQE of up to 29.8%, and an operational T₅₀ of
128.2 h—are among the best reported for pure-red PeLEDs and highlight the technological relevance of the approach. The
manuscript further benefits from a broad and well-integrated set of spectroscopic analyses (TRPL, TA, temperature-
dependent PL, Raman), providing multi-angle evidence for weakened EP interactions. Overall, the work represents a
significant and timely contribution to advancing perovskite NPL-based optoelectronics.
While this work has many merits, we believe that several fundamental issues require further clarification and supporting
evidence.
Regarding these points, I comment on points below.
<Lack of quantitative evaluation of AEBS incorporation>
Although FTIR and XPS analyses confirm AEBS adsorption, the manuscript does not offer quantitative information regarding
the extent of ligand exchange. The relative proportions of AEBS and native OLA ligands remain unclear.
To substantiate the mechanistic claims, quantitative measurements (e.g., TGA, quantitative NMR, or XPS ratio analysis)
should be provided to determine the ligand coverage and the AEBS/OLA ratio.
<Generalizability and mechanistic clarity of the SBA-15 assisted slow-release method>
The use of SBA-15 as a slow-release matrix to mitigate structural degradation during AEBS treatment is intriguing, but its
generality remains ambiguous. It is unclear whether this approach applies to other highly polar or rigid ligands.
Additionally, evidence for the AEBS release kinetics from SBA-15 is absent. Providing adsorption/desorption profiles or
release-time dependence would greatly strengthen the methodological section.
<Insufficient discussion of broader electronic and interfacial effects>
Beyond EP coupling suppression, AEBS—owing to its strong polarity and rigid structure—may influence trap densities,
surface dipoles, and ion migration. UPS data suggest modifications to energy alignment, yet the manuscript does not fully
explore the broader electronic implications.
A more detailed analysis separating EP-related effects from defect passivation and ion-transport effects would provide a
more complete and accurate interpretation of the results.
<Limited insights into device degradation pathways>

Q4. In AEBS-NPLs, weakened EPC suppresses exciton dissociation and increases
exciton binding energy. This should reduce the PL lifetimes and the average lifetimes
when exciton recombination dominates. The authors should clarify this point.
Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We agree that, in general, an
increased E is expected to enhance radiative recombination and shorten the PL lifetime
b
when exciton recombination dominates. However, in strongly quantum-confined NPL
systems, the recombination kinetics may be influenced by more complex factors.
In this system, the recombination dynamics are simultaneously regulated by EP
coupling through both radiative and non-radiative pathways. Based on PLQY and TRPL
analyses (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Table 2), AEBS treatment leads to a significant
reduction in the nonradiative rate (k ) from 0.0238 to 0.0115 ns-1, accompanied by an
nr
increase in the radiative rate (k ) from 0.0406 to 0.0426 ns-1. It should be emphasized
r
that in perovskites, defect trapping and exciton dissociation are typical phonon-assisted
processes, the rates of which are closely related to the EP coupling strength (Nano-
Micro Lett., 2024, 16, 178). Therefore, the weakening of EP coupling itself can
significantly inhibit phonon-assisted carrier trapping, thereby reducing non-radiative
recombination.
Furthermore, in strongly confined systems, the radiative recombination rate is not
solely determined by the electron-hole wavefunction overlap and may also be partially
influenced by phonon-mediated transfer between bright and dark exciton states (Nano
Lett., 2020, 20, 7321; Nano Lett., 2022, 17, 7011; Nat. Commun., 2023, 14, 2426; Adv.
Sci., 2022, 9, 2103013). Therefore, this may account for the lack of a significant
increase in the radiative recombination rate. The extended lifetime in AEBS-NPLs
primarily originates from the inhibition of phonon-assisted non-radiative processes due
to the weakened EP coupling, which is internally consistent with our proposed EP
coupling regulation mechanism. Notably, the coexistence of higher exciton binding
energy and extended PL lifetime in perovskites has been previously reported (Angew.
Chem. Int. Ed., 2024, 63, e202318777; Nat. Nanotechnol., 2025, 20, 507; Adv. Funct.
Mater., 2024, 2311554).

Q6. The manuscript states that both Joule heating and electric-field-induced
degradation are significantly suppressed. Could the authors elaborate on the mechanism
behind this suppression?
Reply:
Reduced Joule heating can be attributed to the mitigated EP coupling and
improved energy-level alignment. Weakened EP coupling enhances carrier mobility
and suppresses phonon-assisted trapping (Fig. 3a-f). Meanwhile, the improved energy-
level alignment reduces the hole-injection barrier and facilitates more balanced charge
injection (Fig. 3a,b and Supplementary Figs. 24,30). Together, these effects effectively
lower the device series resistance (Adv. Mater., 2024, 37, 2412041; Nat. Rev. Chem.,
2025, 9, 261; Nat. Commun., 2016, 7, 11755; ACS Energy Lett., 2017, 2, 1539; Nat.
Commun., 2023, 14, 6441), mitigate nonradiative recombination losses (ACS Nano
2016, 10, 9992; Nat. Photon., 2022, 16, 485; Adv. Mater., 2023, 35, 2209002; Nat.
Commun., 2020, 11, 2712; Nano Lett., 2018, 18, 6645; ACS Nano 2019, 13, 11433),
and consequently suppress Joule heating.
The suppression of electric-field-induced degradation is fundamentally linked to
the inhibition of halide ion migration and enhanced structural integrity. AEBS-NPLs
exhibit a significantly higher ion migration activation energy of 184 meV compared to
106 meV for Control-NPLs (Fig. R5), thereby hindering ion migration (Nat. Photon.,
2017, 11, 726; Nat. Energy, 2020, 5, 131; Nat. Nanotechnol., 2024, 19, 638).
Meanwhile, weakened EP coupling and improved energy-level alignment reduce series
resistance and nonradiative losses, thereby alleviating the impact of Joule heating on
ion migration (Supplementary Fig. 39; Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 6561). In addition,
the rigid vertical anchoring of AEBS ligands on the NPL surface constrains neighboring
ligand motion and lattice fluctuations (Fig. 1b), suppressing local structural
rearrangements and avoiding perovskite degradation under high electric fields.

Reply:
In response to the reviewer’s comment, we provide the following additional
clarification. The observed 0.2-0.3 V reduction in turn-on voltage can be ascribed to the
synergistic effects of balanced carrier injection, efficient transport, and reduced
nonradiative losses (Nature 2018, 562, 245; Sci. Adv., 2024, 10, eadp8473; Light Sci.
Appl., 2025, 14, 50). After AEBS post-treatment, the interfacial energy-level alignment
was optimized (Supplementary Fig. 30), thereby lowering the hole injection barrier
and enabling more balanced charge injection and radiative recombination at lower
voltages. In parallel, the rigid AEBS ligands pin surface OLA conformations, which
weakens EP coupling, reduces carrier-phonon scattering, and enhances carrier mobility
under low electric fields (Supplementary Table 1). Building on the improved injection
and transport, the suppressed EP coupling, together with the reduced defect density,
inhibits phonon-assisted trap capture and nonradiative recombination, thereby lowering
the carrier density threshold required for efficient radiative recombination. Collectively,
these effects account for the reduced turn-on voltage, consistent with the faster response
observed in Tr-EL measurements (Fig. 4h). We thank the reviewer for the comment
and have supplemented the manuscript accordingly.

We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We agree that directly resolving
the precise orientation of organic ligands on NPL surfaces is important. However, due
to the limitations of current experimental techniques, the ligand geometry at the atomic
scale still cannot be unambiguously determined under realistic surface coverage
conditions. Consequently, ligand configurations on the nanocrystals are generally
inferred from density functional theory (DFT) calculations and further validated by
spectroscopic evidence (Fig. R8, Science 2024, 384, 189; Nature 2024, 631, 73; Nature
2023, 5, 830; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2025, e19659; Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 9211).
Following this established framework, our DFT calculations systematically compare
possible binding motifs of AEBS on the CsPbI NPL surface and identify the head-end
3

This configuration involves simultaneous coordination between the sulfonyl group and
surface Pb2+ ions, as well as hydrogen bonding between −NH groups and surface I-
2

backbone. XPS and FTIR analyses further support this assignment by confirming the
expected coordination environment and hydrogen-bonding interactions at the NPL-

conformational order (Fig. R9, Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 9211; J. Am. Chem. Soc.,
2020, 142, 13051; J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1999, 121, 5319; Molecules 2020, 25, 5633; J.
Am. Chem. Soc., 1987, 109, 3559). Upon AEBS treatment, the ν (CH )/ν (CH )
as 2 s 2
intensity ratio decreases, accompanied by a systematic shift to lower wavenumbers and
narrowing of both vibrational bands (Fig. 1e). These spectral changes are well-
established signatures of enhanced alkyl chain order and suppressed conformational
dynamics of OLA ligands.

surface passivation by AEBS, rather than the proposed "pinning" of OLA ligands? The

Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment on distinguishing surface defect
passivation from rigid-ligand pinning. To decouple these two effects, we designed
systematic control experiments using oleylammonium iodide (OLAI) and 3-Amino-1-
propanesulfonamide (APSA). OLAI treatment increases the surface coverage of OLA
and effectively passivates surface defects without introducing new ligand species (Fig.
R10a,b). In contrast, APSA shares the same head and tail functional groups as AEBS
but lacks a rigid aromatic backbone, serving as a flexible analogue to isolate the role of
ligand rigidity (Fig. R10c,d). As shown in Fig. R11, both OLAI-NPLs and APSA-NPLs
exhibit higher PLQYs than Control-NPLs, confirming effective defect passivation.
However, their PL linewidths remain largely unchanged, indicating that defect
passivation alone does not lead to emission narrowing. FTIR analysis further reveals
that both increasing OLA coverage and introducing a flexible APSA ligand fail to
restrict the conformational freedom of the alkyl chains (Fig. R12 and Fig. 1e).
Temperature-dependent PL linewidth fitting shows that Γ slightly increases for
LO
OLAI-NPLs compared to Control-NPLs due to the higher density of long-chain OLA,
whereas Γ for APSA-NPLs shows only a minor reduction compared to Control-NPLs
LO
and remains significantly larger than that of AEBS-NPLs (Fig. R13 and Fig. 2i). These
results demonstrate that flexible ligands or increased surface passivation alone cannot
effectively suppress EP coupling, and that rigid AEBS ligand pinning plays a dominant
role in doing so.

reproducibility and the representativeness of the champion device.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the careful examination of the EQE statistics and
device-to-device variation. The reported EQE statistics are compiled from devices
independently fabricated across multiple batches over an extended period, rather than
from a single optimized experiment. It is important to note that perovskite
optoelectronic properties are intrinsically sensitive to surface states and processing
conditions. In addition, in our system, precise control of the AEBS/SBA-15 ligand post-
treatment process remains challenging. These factors inevitably introduce batch-to-
batch variability under practical fabrication conditions and thereby induce performance
variation. Despite this variability, the devices exhibit an average EQE of 23.2±2.4%,
with all devices outperforming the best Control-NPLs based PeLEDs. The maximum
EQE of 29.8% lies within the continuous tail of the statistical distribution rather than
representing an isolated outlier, with a substantial fraction of devices exceeding 25%.
Similar EQE statistical distributions have also been widely reported in many previously
reported high-performance LEDs (Fig. R14, Nat. Commun., 2019, 10, 3624; Nat.
Photon., 2025, 19, 952; Nat. Commun., 2023, 14, 397; Nature 2021, 591, 72),
supporting the representativeness and reproducibility of the results.

Q5. The improved device performance is primarily attributed to suppressed EP coupling.
However, other factors—such as enhanced surface passivation, improved energy level
alignment, or reduced defect density—could also or more significantly contribute to
these improvements. How can the authors deconvolve the contribution of suppressed
EP coupling from other beneficial effects of AEBS treatment?
Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s professional suggestion to deconvolve the multiple
physical factors influenced by AEBS. To rigorously isolate the specific contribution of
EP coupling suppression, we designed a systematic comparative study: (1) defect-
passivated NPLs using OLAI without introducing new ligand species (OLAI-NPLs);
(2) NPLs treated with APSA (APSA-NPLs) which shares same head and tail functional
groups as AEBS but lacks a rigid backbone (Fig. R10).
OLAI-NPLs exhibit effective defect passivation (Fig. R11b). However, FTIR
analysis shows that the increased surface coverage of OLA ligands enhances
conformational disorder (Fig. R12) and the resulting EP coupling (Fig. R13c).
Moreover, OLAI-NPLs show no significant narrowing of the emission linewidth, nor
do they exhibit improvements in electrical conductivity or device EQE relative to the
control samples (Figs. R11a, R15a, and R16a). These results demonstrate that defect
passivation alone cannot account for the substantial performance enhancement
observed for AEBS-modified devices.
APSA possesses the same head and tail functional groups as AEBS but lacks a
rigid backbone. Unlike AEBS, the APSA fails to effectively suppress the
conformational freedom of the alkyl chains, do not significantly reduce the EP coupling
strength, and also do not exhibit substantial improvements in electrical conductivity or
device EQE (Figs. R12, R13d, R15b and R16b). These findings effectively rule out the
possibility that other chemical contributions of AEBS, such as its short-chain nature
and defect passivation by the functional groups, are the primary drivers of the observed
substantial performance improvement.
In contrast, only the rigid AEBS treatment achieves substantial EP coupling
suppression, which we identify as the dominant mechanism for suppressing exciton
dissociation, reducing carrier-phonon scattering, and achieving narrow emission and
enhanced mobility. In addition, AEBS pinning suppresses lattice vibrations and local
structural rearrangements (Fig. 1b), enhancing lattice stability. EP coupling suppression
further promotes efficient charge transport and reduces nonradiative recombination,
which lowers Joule heating (Supplementary Fig. 39), mitigates ion migration, and
enhances device stability.
Although AEBS modification optimizes energy-level alignment, promotes
balanced charge injection, and lowers the turn-on voltage (Fig.4d), the simultaneous
improvements in device efficiency, operational stability, and emission linewidth
correlate more strongly with the pronounced enhancements in the intrinsic optical
properties, electrical conductivity, and stability of the AEBS-NPLs. Energy-level
alignment alone is insufficient to account for such a substantial and concerted
enhancement, indicating that it is not the primary driving factor for the improved device
performance. Instead, the effective suppression of EP coupling plays a dominant role
and, in synergy with energy-level optimization and defect passivation, endows the
devices with superior optoelectronic performance.
The relevant data have been included in the Supplementary Information
(Supplementary Figs. 25 and 37), and the manuscript has been correspondingly
expanded.

Q6. The interpretation of hot-carrier cooling based on TRPL and TA is indirect. The
rise times in TRPL are influenced by multiple factors, such as trap-assisted processes
or dielectric screening, not solely EP coupling.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments on ultrafast spectroscopic
dynamics. We agree that the rise times observed in TRPL and TA are influenced by
multiple factors. To address this, we performed additional detailed characterizations to
identify the dominant factors governing the rise times in this NPL system.
To address whether defects affect the rise time, we first performed power-
dependent transient absorption (TA) measurements under low pump fluence, where a
low pump fluence was deliberately employed to avoid interference from Auger
recombination and phonon bottleneck effects. If the rise-time difference were governed
by trap states, a clear fluence dependence would be expected (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.
2022, 61, e202111443; J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2019, 141, 3532). However, the rise time
shows negligible fluence dependence (Fig. R17a-f), indicating that trap states are not
the dominant factor controlling the observed rise-time variation. Further support is
provided by comparative experiments on OLAI-NPLs. Although effective defect
passivation is achieved, the increased OLA coverage enhances alkyl-chain disorder and
strengthens EP coupling (Figs. R11b, R12, R13c), leading to an even shorter TA rise
time compared with Control-NPLs (Fig. R17g). Taken together, these results rule out
defects as the primary factor governing the rise time in the ultrafast spectroscopic
dynamics.
Regarding dielectric screening effects, further clarification is provided. The
limited surface coverage of AEBS on the NPLs suggests that its modulation of Coulomb
interactions within the perovskite is expected to be weak. Moreover, previous studies
have reported that even ligands with substantially different dipole moments yield nearly
identical hot-carrier cooling dynamics, indicating that electrostatic or dielectric effects
make a negligible contribution (Nat. Commun., 2017, 8, 1300). Further support is
provided by comparative experiments on APSA-NPLs. APSA lacks an aromatic ring
and thus cannot effectively pin OLA ligands, resulting in ineffective suppression of EP
coupling (Figs. R12 and R13d). APSA shares the same head and tail functional groups
as AEBS; although it does not provide comparable dielectric screening, it can serve as
a reference. Consistently, APSA-NPLs show no significant prolongation of the rise time
in TA dynamics compared with Control-NPLs, further excluding dielectric screening as
the dominant origin of the observed dynamical changes (Fig. R17h).
The relevant data have been included in the Supplementary Information
(Supplementary Fig. 18), and the manuscript has been correspondingly expanded.

Q7. The SCLC measurements show that the mobility in AEBS-NPLs increased, but the
analysis did not distinguish between the decrease of EP coupling and other factors, such
as the improved film morphology or the reduced trap density.
Reply:
To deconvolve the multiple factors that may influence carrier mobility, we
performed additional comparative analyses combining structural characterization with
carefully designed control experiments.
SEM and AFM characterizations in Supplementary Fig. 31 show that AEBS-
NPLs and Control-NPLs exhibit no intrinsic differences in film continuity, surface
roughness, or overall morphology. These results exclude morphology-driven transport
improvement as the dominant origin of enhanced mobility.
We further conducted control experiments analogous to those discussed in Q5.
OLAI treatment primarily induces defect passivation; however, the charge-transport
capability of OLAI-NPLs shows no significant improvement compared with that of
Control-NPLs (Fig. R15a and Fig. 3c). Similarly, APSA, which is structurally
analogous to AEBS but lacks a rigid backbone, cannot effectively pin OLA ligands and
fails to efficiently suppress EP coupling. APSA-NPLs present a modest increase in
conductivity, which remains much weaker than that observed in AEBS-NPLs. (Fig.
R15b and Fig. 3c).
These comparative results demonstrate that the potential defect passivation effect
of functional groups and the short-chain nature of AEBS are insufficient to account for
the substantial mobility enhancement observed in AEBS-NPLs. When considered
together with the pronounced suppression of EP coupling, they indicate that the
significantly improved mobility in AEBS-NPLs primarily originates from reduced
carrier scattering associated with weakened EP coupling.
The relevant data have been included in the Supplementary Information
(Supplementary Fig. 25), and the manuscript has been correspondingly
expanded.

Q2. <Generalizability and mechanistic clarity of the SBA-15 assisted slow-release
method>

Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. In response, we have conducted
further supplementary experiments.
SBA-15, as a well-established biomedical sustained-release carrier (Angew. Chem.
Int. Ed., 2007, 46, 7548; J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2006, 128, 8116), exhibits the potential to
accommodate highly polar ligands. Therefore, the use of SBA-15 for the sustained
release of polar ligands is not limited to AEBS alone. However, the efficacy of this
strategy in mitigating perovskite structural degradation during post-treatment remains
dependent on factors such as ligand polarity and solvent affinity. Consequently, each
specific ligand system requires case-by-case evaluation.
To address the reviewer’s concern regarding insufficient evidence for the release
kinetics of AEBS from SBA-15, the nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms of
pristine SBA-15 and AEBS-loaded SBA-15 composites (Fig. R19; Supplementary Fig.

indicate that AEBS partially occupies and blocks the mesopores of SBA-15 rather than
being merely adsorbed on the external surface. In addition, we directly probed the
release behavior of AEBS from SBA-15 by monitoring the time-dependent PL
evolution in solution (Fig. R20). In this experiment, AEBS powder and AEBS/SBA-15
composite powder were separately placed at the bottom of cuvettes filled with hexane,
and the PL intensity of the supernatant was continuously monitored as a function of
time to track AEBS release. Compared with AEBS, the AEBS/SBA-15 exhibits a
markedly slower increase in PL intensity, demonstrating a significantly reduced release
rate under the regulation of SBA-15.

Q4. While the reported operational stability is excellent, the manuscript provides little
mechanistic insight into degradation processes.
Analyses such as EL spectral evolution under bias, voltage rise during operation, or ion
migration-related signatures would help clarify the origin of the improved device
lifetime and reinforce the claims of structural stabilization.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the professional suggestion. For PeLEDs, performance
degradation is closely linked to electric- and thermally driven ion migration in
perovskites as well as the stability of the perovskite lattice structure (Nat. Nanotechnol.,
2024, 19, 638; ACS Energy Lett., 2019, 4, 779; Acc. Chem. Res., 2016, 49, 286; ACS
Nano, 2016, 10, 693; Nature, 2024, 631, 73).
We investigated the mechanism underlying the suppression of electric-field-
induced degradation. The evolution of the EL spectra under different driving voltages
reveals a pronounced spectral broadening in Control-NPLs based PeLEDs (Fig. R27a),
which is attributed to severe halide ion migration (Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 6561). Ion
migration induces lattice degradation and increased interfacial energy barriers, leading
to a rise in operating voltage and substantial Joule heating under constant-current
operation (Fig. R27b) (Nat. Photon., 2021, 15, 630). In contrast, AEBS-NPLs exhibit
a higher activation energy (E ) for ion migration (Fig. R28), which hinders ion
a
migration (Nat. Photon., 2017, 11, 726; Nat. Energy 2020, 5, 131; Nat. Nanotechnol.,
2024, 19, 638), and the AEBS pinning effect suppresses lattice vibrations and local
structural rearrangements, thereby enhancing lattice stability (Fig. 1b). In addition,
weakened EP coupling and improved energy-level alignment reduce series resistance
and nonradiative losses, thereby alleviating the impact of Joule heating on ion migration
(Supplementary Fig. 39; Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 6561). Collectively, these factors
result in a substantial enhancement of device operational lifetime.
The relevant data have been added to the Supplementary Information (Supplementary
Figs. 32,38,40), and the corresponding analysis has been included in the main
manuscript.

Q5. <Oversimplified attribution of emission broadening in the control NPLs>
The authors attribute the broader emission linewidth of the control sample primarily to
enhanced EP coupling. However, other factors, including trap-mediated recombination,
surface reconstruction, and OLA desorption, are also likely contributors, particularly in
light of the stability data presented in the SI.
A more nuanced discussion acknowledging these additional mechanisms is
recommended
Reply:
We systematically analyzed the mechanisms governing emission linewidth
broadening. TEM characterization revealed that the Control-NPLs and AEBS-NPLs are
highly consistent in terms of thickness uniformity (Fig. R29 and Fig. 1c), effectively
ruling out thickness inhomogeneity as the dominant factor responsible for the linewidth
difference. Control experiments using OLAI demonstrated that, despite enhancing
surface OLA coverage, effectively passivating iodine vacancies, and repairing the
surface structure, these treatments did not induce a significant narrowing of the
emission linewidth (Fig. R22a). This indicates that defect passivation or surface
reconstruction is not the primary source of the observed linewidth difference.
Furthermore, at ~80 K, EP coupling contributes minimally, and Control-NPLs and
AEBS-NPLs show comparable emission linewidths (Fig. 2i). With increasing
temperature, EP coupling induced broadening becomes dominant, particularly in
Control-NPLs, indicating that their broader linewidth primarily arises from stronger EP
coupling.

We thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation of our work. Detailed point-by-
point responses to the comments are provided below.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript has been substantially improved. However, two points require clarification before acceptance.
1.Please provide quantitative thickness and lateral size distribution statistics to exclude the possibility that the linewidth
narrowing arises from reduced inhomogeneous broadening.
2.Although AEBS modification clearly mitigates efficiency roll-off at high current density, the manuscript should explicitly
discuss the origins of this improvement.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have addressed most of my concerns. I would like to recommend acceptance of the revised paper for
publication.

### Reviewer 3

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 4

I thank the authors for their thorough and constructive responses to my previous comments.
The revised manuscript and the expanded Supplementary Information have significantly strengthened both the mechanistic
analysis and the overall clarity of the work.
Q1 – Quantification of AEBS incorporation.
The addition of TGA, ¹H NMR analysis, and XPS characterization substantially improves the description of the ligand
environment after AEBS treatment. While the determination of absolute surface coverage remains semi-quantitative, the
reported OLA/AEBS ratio and ligand density analysis are sufficient to support the proposed surface-modulation mechanism
within the scope of this study.
Q2 – Validity of the SBA-15 slow-release strategy.
The release-dependent PL measurements and BET characterization reasonably demonstrate that SBA-15 moderates ligand
delivery and prevents structural degradation during post-treatment. Although a fully quantitative release-kinetics analysis is
not provided, the experimental evidence adequately supports the functional role of the slow-release strategy.
Q3 – Evidence for suppression of electron–phonon coupling.
The clarified linewidth fitting procedure, explicit reporting of ΓLO values, Huang–Rhys factor extraction using the MBO
model, and supporting TA and Raman analyses collectively provide a coherent and internally consistent mechanistic
picture. While complete disentanglement of defect passivation and EP-coupling effects is intrinsically challenging, the
presented data sufficiently substantiate EP-coupling suppression as a dominant contributing factor.
Q4 – Device stability mechanism.
The addition of ion-migration activation energy measurements and temperature-dependent analyses convincingly connects
materials-level modification with device-level stability enhancement. This aspect has been substantially strengthened in the
revision.
Q5 – Exclusion of alternative explanations for linewidth narrowing.
Control experiments using OLAI and APSA provide reasonable comparative evidence that defect passivation alone cannot
account for the observed linewidth narrowing. Minor wording adjustments may be advisable to avoid overly exclusive
statements, but no further experimental evidence is required.
Overall, my primary scientific concerns have been adequately addressed. The manuscript now presents a well-supported
mechanism linking ligand rigidity, suppressed electron–phonon coupling, and improved PeLED performance.

## Paper

## Abstract

Perovskite light-emitting diodes are promising for next-generation ultrahigh-definition displays, yet efficient pure-red emission (620-650 nm) with high spectral purity remains challenging, with emission linewidths commonly exceeding 30 nm. CsPbI3 nanoplatelets feature the potential for narrow-linewidth emission owing to strong vertical quantum confinement and atomic-level flat surface. Nonetheless, the dynamic motion of native long-chain oleylamine exacerbates lattice vibrations in ultrathin soft lattices, inducing strong electron-phonon coupling and undermining optical advantages. Here, we introduce the rigid 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonamide molecule, which partially replaces oleylamine and vertically anchors on the nanoplatelets, sterically restricting the dynamic motion of neighboring oleylamine, thereby mitigating electron-phonon coupling. The resulting light-emitting diodes achieve pure-red electroluminescence at 641 nm with a narrow linewidth of 24 nm, an average external quantum efficiency of 23.2 ± 2.4% (maximum 29.8%), and an operational lifetime of 128.2 h. This work underscores the critical role of electron-phonon coupling modulation in optimizing perovskite optoelectronic devices.

---

## Introduction

Perovskite materials possess tunable bandgaps, high photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs), and can be fabricated via low-cost solution processes, making perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) promising for advanced display technologies1-11. Although considerable progress has been made in improving external quantum efficiency (EQE)1,6,12, pure-red PeLEDs still face key challenges. These devices are typically based on Br/I mixed-halide perovskites5,13,14, tending to undergo ion migration and phase segregation under device operation15. This instability results in emission redshift and spectral broadening, which hinder the realization of narrow electroluminescence (EL) full width at half maximum (FWHM)16. As a result, their practical use in next-generation display technologies remains limited. Quantum-confined low-dimensional pure-iodide based perovskites offer an effective solution to circumvent the above challenges. Among them, quasi-2D films and small-sized quantum dots are the most widely studied systems4,6,17. However, the rapid nucleation and growth kinetics process hinders size uniformity, causing inhomogeneous emission broadening (FWHM > 30 nm) due to multi-center recombination18,19. By contrast, the perovskite nanoplatelets (NPLs) exhibit distinct structural advantages. The thermodynamic preference against vertical growth in NPLs yields atomically flat basal planes, characterized by uniform thickness20. Given that their emission is primarily determined by strong vertical quantum confinement and is relatively insensitive to lateral size variations, NPLs intrinsically favor narrowband emission20-27.

Despite these merits, pure-red NPLs-based PeLEDs still suffer from broad EL linewidths and unsatisfactory device performances28,29. This limitation primarily stems from the ultrathin geometry of NPLs, which amplifies the inherent lattice softness of perovskites, increasing susceptibility to structural fluctuations20,30-35. Furthermore, the long-chain oleylamine (OLA) ligands, essential for stabilizing the layered structure, introduce significant dynamic disorder due to high conformational freedom, thereby exacerbating lattice vibrations20,36,37 (Fig. 1a). The resulting strong electron-phonon (EP) coupling intensifies non-radiative recombination, promotes carrier scattering, and broadens emission linewidths, ultimately constraining the potential of NPLs for high-performance LEDs30,35,36,38-42.

In this work, we design a rigid-ligand pinning strategy using 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonamide (AEBS) (Fig. 1a). The rigid AEBS molecules vertically anchor on NPL surfaces and sterically restrict the dynamic motion of neighboring OLA ligands, thereby mitigating OLA-aggravated EP coupling. This enables high-performance PeLED devices with a maximum EQE and an operational lifetime of 29.8% and 128.2 h, respectively. Our work may inspire the design of NPLs for optoelectronic applications.

---

## Results

Effect of rigid ligand pinning

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that AEBS adopts a nearly perpendicular configuration on the NPLs surface through strong coordination of sulfonyl (−S(=O)2−) group with Pb2+ ions and −NH2 groups with I- (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Figure 1). The rigid and upright molecular geometry on the NPLs surface sterically restricts the dynamic motion of adjacent OLA ligands (Supplementary Figure 2), effectively reducing ligand-induced lattice vibrations. Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate the smaller temporal variations in the bond length of Pb−I in AEBS-treated NPLs (AEBS-NPLs, ~2.9-3.2 Å) compared to those without AEBS anchoring (Control-NPLs, ~2.9-3.6 Å) (Fig. 1b), indicating a more stable inorganic [PbI6]4- octahedral framework.

Due to the high polarity of AEBS, direct post-treatment leads to rapid ligand exchange and structural degradation of perovskites, inducing NPLs aggregation and severe photoluminescence (PL) quenching (Supplementary Figure 3). Herein, we pre-load AEBS molecules into mesoporous silica (SBA‑15) as a slow‑release medium (Supplementary Figures 4-7). This controlled delivery retained structural integrity and square platelet morphology of NPLs during post-treatment (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Figures 8-13). As shown in Fig. 1d, AEBS-NPLs exhibit a sharp emission peak centered at 640 nm with a FWHM of ~24 nm, representing the narrowest PL linewidth reported for Pb-based pure-red perovskite to date1,4,6,9,43. The ligand pinning effect of AEBS is further supported by Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. The νas(CH2) and νs(CH2) vibrational bands are highly sensitive to the conformational order of hydrocarbon chains. Compared with Control-NPLs, AEBS-NPLs exhibit a marked decrease in the νas(CH2)/νs(CH2) intensity ratio and a pronounced shift of both bands to lower wavenumbers, accompanied by reductions in their fitted bandwidths, indicating enhanced alkyl-chain ordering and suppressed conformational dynamics of the OLA ligand44-46 (Fig. 1e). Oleylammonium iodide (OLAI) and 3-Amino-1-propanesulfonamide (APSA) are introduced to clarify the role of ligand structure. OLAI increases OLA surface coverage and passivates defects without introducing new ligand species, whereas APSA possesses the same head and tail groups as AEBS but lacks a rigid aromatic backbone (Supplementary Figures 14 and 15). The more pronounced alkyl-chain disorder induced by higher OLAI content and the limited conformational constraint of APSA collectively underscore the pinning effect of rigid ligands (Supplementary Figure 16).

Modulation of electron-phonon coupling by ligands

To further elucidate the effect of AEBS ligands on EP coupling in CsPbI3 NPLs, we conduct a comprehensive set of transient and steady-state spectroscopic measurements. Since strong EP coupling accelerates hot carrier cooling and increases energy loss, hot carrier relaxation dynamics serve as a sensitive probe to evaluate EP interactions.47-50. We first examine the early-stage relaxation process via time-resolved PL (TRPL), where the initial rise in TRPL traces reflects the dephasing of initial polarization and the hot carrier relaxation51,52. As shown in Fig. 2a-c and Supplementary Figure 17, the temperature-dependent rise rate (k_rise) of both NPLs follows a power-law dependence k_rise ∝ T^γ (γ > 0). A markedly lower exponent for AEBS-NPLs (γ = 0.89) compared to Control-NPLs (γ = 1.29) is to some extent associated with the weaker EP interaction in AEBS-NPLs41,51 (Fig. 2c). Consistent results are provided by the prolonged rise time of the ground-state bleach (GSB) in transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy, which increases from 0.73 ps in Control-NPLs to 1.43 ps in AEBS-NPLs (Fig. 2d-f and Supplementary Figure 18). Further, the slower hot carrier temperature (Tc) dynamics decay and narrower Raman peaks provide strong evidence for weaker EP interaction in AEBS-NPLs47,48,53-57 (Supplementary Figures 19 and 20). Finally, temperature-dependent steady-state PL measurements provide quantitative evaluation of EP coupling strength. As shown in Fig. 2g-i and Supplementary Figure 21, the dominant PL peak in AEBS-NPLs exhibits a smaller linewidth variation with increasing temperature (from 80 K to 300 K) compared to that in Control-NPLs. Fitting the temperature-dependent linewidth variation reveals that AEBS-NPLs exhibit the lowest exciton-longitudinal optical (LO) phonon coupling strength (Γ_LO) of 36.6 meV (Fig. 2i and Supplementary Figure 22).The markedly lower Γ_LO in AEBS-NPLs indicates that AEBS modification effectively suppresses EP coupling, accounting for the narrow emission linewidth of the AEBS-NPLs30,54,58 (Fig. 1d), in agreement with the reduced Huang-Rhys factor (S) (Supplementary Figure 23).

Enhanced optoelectronic properties

EP coupling in CsPbI3 NPLs plays a critical role in governing their electrical and optical behavior. Space-charge-limited current (SCLC) measurements reveal that both electron and hole mobilities are markedly increased in AEBS-treated NPLs compared to Control-NPLs (Fig. 3a,b and Supplementary Figure 24). Consistently, the electrical conductivity (σ) of AEBS-NPLs film reaches 9.42 × 10-6 S m-1, 2.2-fold higher than that of Control-NPLs (4.25 × 10-6 S m-1) (Fig. 3c). These improvements are primarily attributed to suppressed carrier scattering due to weakened EP coupling, further assisted by the structural advantages of the short-chain conjugated AEBS ligands and defect passivation30,35,38,59 (Supplementary Figure 25 and Supplementary Table 1). Moreover, optical characterizations further underscore the benefits of EP coupling suppression. As shown in Figs. 2g,h and 3d, the weakened EP coupling in AEBS-NPLs suppresses exciton dissociation, thereby achieving a high exciton binding energy (Eb) and effectively preventing thermal degradation60,61. In addition, the combination of AEBS passivation and weakened EP coupling effectively reduces non-radiative recombination (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2), leading to an overall improvement in PLQYs51,55,58,62 (Fig. 3f). These combined effects endow AEBS-NPLs with superior structural and photophysical robustness under diverse operational and environmental conditions (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Figures 26-29).

Electroluminescence performance and operational stability

Encouraged by the enhanced optoelectronic properties, we further fabricate PeLEDs with a multi-layer structure of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/PTAA/NPLs/TPBi/LiF/Al (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Figures 30 and 31). The AEBS-NPLs based PeLEDs deliver voltage-invariant EL spectra centered at ~641 nm, featuring the narrowest EL linewidth of ~24 nm among all the reported Pb-based pure-red PeLEDs (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Figure 32 and Supplementary Table 3). The corresponding Commission Internationale de l’Eclairage (CIE) chromaticity coordinates of (0.702, 0.296) satisfy the Rec.2020 standard, outperforming the control device (Supplementary Figure 33). Angle-dependent EL intensity follows a Lambertian profile (Fig. 4c). The current density-voltage-luminance (J-V-L) and EQE-J characteristics of a representative AEBS-NPLs based PeLED demonstrate a maximum EQE of 23.7% and a maximum luminance (L_max) of 2,060 cd m-2. In contrast, the control device achieves a significantly lower EQE of 9.5% and L_max of 550 cd m-2 (Fig. 4d,e). AEBS-NPLs based PeLEDs exhibit suppressed efficiency roll-off, arising from weakened EP coupling that mitigates exciton dissociation induced quenching and improved energy-level alignment that promotes balanced charge injection and suppresses Auger recombination7,60,61 (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Figure 30). Statistical analysis of 30 devices reveals a distribution of EQE ranging from 19.3% to 29.8% for AEBS-NPLs based PeLEDs, with an average of 23.2 ± 2.4% (Supplementary Figures 34-36). In comparison, PeLEDs based on OLAI-NPLs and APSA-NPLs achieve limited EQE enhancement (Supplementary Figure 37). A summary of reported EQEs and EL linewidths for pure-red PeLEDs is provided in Figure 4f and Supplementary Table 3. The operational stability of the devices is further evaluated. Under continuous operation at an initial luminance of ~100 cd m-2, the AEBS-NPLs based device achieves a half-lifetime (T50) of ~128.2 h, ~15-fold longer than the control device (Fig 4g and Supplementary Figure 38). This represents one of the longest operational lifetimes reported for pure-red PeLEDs (Supplementary Table 3). We further investigate the charge dynamics and thermal behavior of the devices to understand the origin of the improved device performance. Transient EL (Tr-EL) reveals that AEBS-NPLs based devices exhibit shorter EL rise times (tr) and fall times (tf) than the control counterparts (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Table 4), indicative of more efficient carrier injection and radiative recombination4,58. These findings are consistent with the higher current density observed at identical biases and the lower turn-on voltage in these devices11 (Fig. 4d). Moreover, thermal imaging reveals that the AEBS-NPLs based device undergoes significantly less Joule heating as voltage increases to 5 V, exhibiting a surface temperature rise of only 5.6 °C, in contrast to 13.9 °C observed in the control device (Supplementary Figure 39). The reduction in Joule heating originates from mitigated EP coupling and improved energy-level alignment, promoting efficient charge injection and transport while reducing series resistance and nonradiative losses. Reduced Joule heating, the elevated ion-migration activation energy, and the stable lattice enabled by AEBS ligand pinning together lead to a marked improvement in the stability of AEBS-NPLs based devices (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Figures 39 and 40).

---

## Methods

Materials

Cesium carbonate (Cs2CO3, 99.9%) and chlorobenzene (C6H5Cl, 99.9%) were purchased from Alfa Aesar. Lead(II) acetate trihydrate (Pb(OAc)2·3H2O, 99.99%), oleylamine (OLA, 80-90%), oleic acid (OA, 90%), ethyl acetate (99.8%), isopropyl alcohol (99.9%), 1-octadecene (ODE, 90%) and 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonamide (AEBS) were purchased from Aladdin. Zinc iodide (ZnI2, 99.99%) and n-hexane (99%) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. The mesoporous particles (SBA-15) were purchased from Nanjing XFNANO Co. Ltd. 1,3,5-Tris(1-phenyl-1H-benzimidazol-2-yl)benzene (TPBi) and lithium fluoride (LiF) were purchased from Luminescence Technology Corp. Poly(ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrenesulfonate (PEDOT:PSS; Heraeus-Clevios PVP AI4083) and poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)amine] (PTAA) were purchased from Xian Yuri Solar Co, Ltd. All chemicals were used directly without any further purification.

Preparation of precursor

Cs2CO3 (0.21 g), Pb(OAc)2·3H2O (0.475 g), OA (2.5 mL) and ODE (10 mL) were loaded into a 50 mL three-necked flask, and the mixture was degassed for 15 min at 100 °C under argon. Subsequently, the mixture was heated at 120 °C under argon atmosphere for 30 minutes until a transparent solution was obtained. The resulting precursor solution was heated at 100 °C under argon before injection.

Preparation of molecule loaded mesoporous silica

To synthesize the nanocomposite, 50 mg of AEBS powder was dissolved in 10 mL of isopropanol, and the SBA-15 was impregnated with the solution, followed by ultrasonication to facilitate the infiltration of the solution into the mesopores. The solid product was then separated, washed three times with isopropanol, and vacuum-dried to obtain the final material.

Synthesis and purification of nanoplatelets

For the typical synthesis of CsPbI3 NPLs, 0.26 g ZnI2, 2.3 mL OA, 1.8 mL OLA and 6 mL ODE were loaded into a 50 mL three-neck flask, which was degassed and dried under vacuum for 30 min at 120 °C. Then the temperature was reduced to 100 °C and 1.5 mL precursor solution was quickly injected. After waiting for 1 min, the reaction mixture was immediately cooled down to room temperature by an ice-water bath.

The crude solution was transferred to a 50 mL centrifuge tube, and 15 mL of ethyl acetate was added. The mixture was centrifuged at 9,800 × g for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded. The precipitate was dissolved in 1 mL of n-hexane, followed by the addition of 3 mL of ethyl acetate. The resulting mixture was centrifuged at 9,800 × g for 5 min, and the precipitate was collected. The precipitate was dissolved in 1 mL of hexane and centrifuged at 2,460 × g for 3 min to retain the supernatant. Ethyl acetate (3 mL) was added to the supernatant, and the mixtures were centrifuged at 9,800 × g for 5 min to isolate the precipitates. Finally, the precipitates were redispersed in n-hexane. AEBS-functionalized NPLs were prepared by ultrasonicating a dispersion of NPLs in n-hexane containing AEBS/SBA-15 (~5 mg). A sonication time of ~3 min was employed to achieve the desired surface AEBS-to-OLA ratio (Supplementary Figure 7). The final product was collected from the supernatant after centrifugation at 9,800 × g for 1 min. For OLAI- and APSA-modified NPLs, the ligand was added to the NPL dispersion in n-hexane, stirred for ~20 min, and centrifuged at 9,800 × g for 1 min to collect the supernatant. All n-hexane solutions containing NPLs are filtered through 0.22 μm PTFE filters. The resulting NPLs solutions were stored for further characterization and LED fabrication.

Device fabrication

PeLEDs were fabricated on ITO-coated glass substrates with a sheet resistance of ~17 Ω sq-1. Before using, these coated substrates were cleaned with deionized water, acetone, and isopropanol for 15 min, respectively. Then these substrates were treated with oxygen plasma for 15 min. A PEDOT:PSS solution was spin-coated onto the ITO substrate at 4,000 rpm for 40 s and then baked at 150 °C for 20 min in ambient air. Subsequently, the ITO substrate was transferred into a nitrogen-filled glovebox. PTAA (8 mg mL-1 in chlorobenzene) was spin-coated onto PEDOT:PSS layer at 4,000 rpm for 40 s, followed by annealing at 120 °C for 20 min. Perovskite was spin-coated at 2,000 rpm for 40 s. After that, TPBi (40-50 nm), LiF (1 nm) and an Al electrode (100 nm) were thermally evaporated with a vacuum pressure below 4 × 10-4 Pa.

Material characterizations

High-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) images and HAADF-STEM images were obtained by Themis Z microscope, and the accelerating voltage was 200 kV. AFM images of NPL films were measured by a Dimension Icon instrument. XRD patterns of perovskite films were obtained using a MiniFlex 600 X-ray diffractometer with a Cu-Kα source (λ = 1.54056 Å). The FTIR spectra of NPLs were measured by an IRTracer-100 Fourier infrared spectrometer. 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) measurements were recorded on a Bruker AVANCE NEO 400 spectrometer. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was carried out using a NETZSCH STA 449 F3 instrument. The samples were heated from 30 °C to 800 °C at a rate of 20 °C·min-1 under a nitrogen flow. Grazing incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) data were collected using an X-ray wavelength of 0.154 nm. XPS and UPS were measured by a spectrometer system (Nexsa G2, Thermo Fisher Scientific). A monochromatic Al Kα line (1,486.6 eV) was used for XPS, and He I radiation (21.2 eV) was used for UPS. The conductivity of a film was measured by a semiconductor parameter analyzer (Keithley, 4200) with a probe station. A 100 nm-thick Au layer was deposited onto a glass/perovskite film by thermal evaporation. Field-effect transistor (FET) exhibits a channel length of 50 μm and a channel width of 1 cm. The thickness of the perovskite film is 30 nm.

Optical characterizations

UV-visible absorption spectra were acquired using a Lambda 1050+ spectrophotometer. The Raman spectra were obtained using a Horiba LabRAMP HR Evolution confocal Raman microscope. A 785 nm laser was used as the excitation source. The PLQY values were measured using a system that included a xenon flash lamp, a QE Pro spectrometer and a custom-built integrating sphere. Temperature-dependent steady-state PL spectra were recorded using a confocal microscope (Witec Alpha300R) equipped with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled cryostat, with a 405 nm laser as the excitation source.

TRPL measurements were conducted with the confocal microscope coupled to a streak camera (C10910, Hamamatsu). A Ti: Sapphire pulsed laser operating at 400 nm (pulse width: 80 fs; repetition rate: 80 MHz) was employed as the excitation source.

Time-resolved TA spectra were acquired using femtosecond broadband pump-probe microscopy. The light source was a regenerative amplifier system (Spitfire-ace, Spectra-Physics) operating at 800 nm with a pulse width of 80 fs and a repetition rate of 250 Hz. The output from the amplifier was divided into two paths; one was frequency-doubled to produce a 400 nm pump beam. The other beam was focused into a sapphire plate (C-cut, 2 mm thick) to form the continuous white light with a range of 450-750 nm as the probe beam. Both beams were directed into a custom-built microscope and focused onto the samples. The sub-picosecond time delay between the pump and probe pulses was controlled using a mechanical delay line (Newport, M-ILS250CC, 250 mm). A spectrometer (Avantes, AvaSpec-2048L) positioned after the microscope was used to capture the transient signals. All measurements were performed under comparable experimental conditions.

Device characterizations

The active area of the device was defined as 4 mm2. Electroluminescence characterization was performed at room temperature in a nitrogen-filled glovebox using a Keithley 2400 source meter coupled with an integrating sphere (50 mm diameter, Shenzhen Pynect) and an Ocean Optics QE Pro spectrometer. The angular dependence of the emission intensity was collected using a Konica Minolta CS-200 detector. The operational lifetimes of PeLEDs were evaluated via a commercial organic LED aging system (ZJZCL-1) in a nitrogen environment. Thermal images of the samples were acquired using a Fluke Ti401 PRO camera. The Tr-EL signal was collected by a high-speed photomultiplier tube (Hamamatsu, H10721-20) and transformed into a current signal. The current signal was sent to a transimpedance amplifier (Femto, DHPCA-100) and then collected by a digital oscilloscope (MXR108B).

The ion-migration activation energy was measured using a FET device architecture. A 10 V bias was applied to the electrodes for ~20 s with a source meter (Keithley 2400) to induce ion migration. Upon abrupt voltage removal, a negative current arising from ion-vacancy redistribution was recorded and decayed exponentially, with its decay reflecting the ionic transport dynamics. Measurements were conducted from 220 to 310 K using a liquid-nitrogen-cooled cryostat. The transient currents were fitted with a double-exponential function, and the slower decay constant (τ), corresponding to the ion redistribution recovery time, was used to extract the activation energy.

Optical simulation

Both random orientation (isotropic dipole distribution) and fully face-down orientation of emitters are assumed in this model. The following optical channels are considered in the simulation: nonradiative mode, surface plasmon polariton (SPP) mode, waveguide mode, absorption mode, substrate mode, and air mode. The air mode corresponds to the theoretically simulated EQE limit.

Density functional theory calculation

In this work, the calculations are conducted within the framework of DFT using Vienna Ab Simulation Package (VASP)63,64. The generalized gradient approximation exchange-correlation function is described by Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE), and the projector augmented wave pseudopotential is introduced with a cutoff of 400 eV (Ref.65). The models are relaxed until the force convergence criterion is less than 0.01 eV Å-1 per atom and the energy convergence criterion is less than 10-5 eV. To avoid the interaction between the two nearest neighbor unit cells, the vacuum is set to 20 Å in the Z-direction. A 4 × 4 × 1 r-centered k-point mesh is used for Brillouin-zone sampling.

Temperature-dependent photoluminescence line fitting

The FWHM of the dominant peak in each temperature-dependent PL spectrum is extracted by deconvoluting the PL spectra and plotted against temperature according to the following equation, enabling the estimation of the EP coupling strength58:

Γ(T)= Γ_inh + Γ_ac T + Γ_LO / (exp(E_LO / (kB T)) − 1) (1)

in which Γ_inh represents the inhomogeneous broadening arising from variation of crystal size, shape, and composition, as well as the scattering process associated with the imperfections of the lattice, Γ_ac is the exciton-acoustic phonon coupling coefficient, Γ_LO denotes the exciton-LO phonon coupling strength, E_LO represents the LO phonon energy and kB is the Boltzmann constant. The two mechanisms of acoustic phonon deformation scattering and Fröhlich interaction with LO phonon are generally responsible for the emergence of EP coupling. In the low-temperature regime (< 110 K), the EP interaction is predominantly governed by acoustic phonons, while high-energy LO phonons dominate this interaction in the high-temperature region. Therefore, the fitting above 110 K mainly considers the Γ_inh and Γ_LO terms, with E_LO constrained within the Raman-determined range to ensure more rigorous and reliable quantification38,39.

Exciton binding energy calculation

The exciton binding energy is determined by fitting the temperature-dependent integrated PL intensities of the dominant emission peak using the Arrhenius equation6:

I(T) = I0 / (1 + A exp(−Eb / (kB T))) (2)

where I0 is the integrated PL intensity at 0 K, Eb is the exciton binding energy, and A is the coefficient.

Carrier mobility calculation

To evaluate the out-of-plane carrier mobility of CsPbI3 NPLs, SCLC measurements are systematically conducted on both EODs and hole-only devices (HODs). The J-V curves of the fabricated devices can be divided into three regions based on the voltage‑dependent slope (k): an ohmic region (k = 1) in the low‑injection regime, a trap‑filled limit (TFL) region (k > 3), and an SCLC region (k = 2). Carrier mobility for each device is calculated from the Mott-Gurney law in the Child regime of trap-free SCLC transport7, as follows:

J = 9/8 εr ε0 μ (V^2 / d^3) (3)

where V is the applied voltage, d is the thickness of film, εr is the relative permittivity of perovskite (6.32 for CsPbI3), ε0 is the vacuum permittivity, and μ is the carrier mobility.

Defect density calculation

The trap-filled limit voltages of HODs and EODs are extracted and combined with the following equation to calculate the total trap state density of the perovskite films6,7:

nt = 2 εr ε0 VTFL / (e d^2) (4)

where nt is the trap state density, VTFL is the trap-filled limit voltage, and e is the elementary charge, respectively.

Conductivity calculation

The σ is calculated using the following equation5,66:

σ = (I / V) × (l / (D × W)) (5)

where l is the channel length, D is the thickness of the film, W is the channel width and I/V is the slope of the current-voltage curve.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript reports a strategy to suppress electron-phonon (EP) coupling in CsPbI₃ nanoplatelets (NPLs) using a rigid
ligand (AEBS) to achieve efficient pure-red light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) with a narrow emission linewidth of 24 nm. While
the study addresses an important topic in perovskite optoelectronics and presents an interesting ligand-pinning concept, the
manuscript suffers from several critical issues that undermine the validity of its central claims and the robustness of its
conclusions. The evidence provided is insufficient to convincingly demonstrate that the observed improvement is primarily
due to the inhibition of EP coupling. Therefore, the manuscript in its current form is not recommended for publication. Below
are specific major concerns that must be adequately addressed:

parameters for quantifying EP coupling, such as the Huang-Rhys factor or direct measurement of phonon modes via ultrafast
spectroscopy, are not provided.

How can the proposed perpendicular configuration be conclusively verified? Meanwhile, the proposed mechanism where
AEBS "pins" dynamic OLA ligands is speculative. No direct experimental evidence is provided.
3. How can the authors rule out that the observed effects are not simply due to superior surface passivation by AEBS,
rather than the proposed "pinning" of OLA ligands? The study lacks a control experiment using a structurally similar but flexible
ligand to isolate the effect of ligand rigidity from other chemical properties.

23.2 ± 2.4%. The large standard deviation suggests significant device-to-device variation, raising a concern about the
reproducibility and the representativeness of the champion device.
5. The improved device performance is primarily attributed to suppressed EP coupling. However, other factors—such as
enhanced surface passivation, improved energy level alignment, or reduced defect density—could also or more significantly
contribute to these improvements. How can the authors deconvolve the contribution of suppressed EP coupling from other
beneficial effects of AEBS treatment?
6. The interpretation of hot-carrier cooling based on TRPL and TA is indirect. The rise times in TRPL are influenced by

the decrease of EP coupling and other factors, such as the improved film morphology or the reduced trap density.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript presents a clear and compelling strategy to suppress electron–phonon (EP) coupling in CsPbI₃
nanoplatelets (NPLs), which has long been a critical bottleneck limiting the spectral purity and device performance of pure-

motif is conceptually strong and addresses the fundamental issue of lattice softness and dynamic disorder originating from
long-chain oleylamine ligands. The authors convincingly demonstrate that AEBS anchoring suppresses lattice vibrations,
reduces EP coupling strength, and narrows both PL and EL linewidths.
Importantly, the achieved device metrics—an EL FWHM of 24 nm, a peak EQE of up to 29.8%, and an operational T₅₀ of
128.2 h—are among the best reported for pure-red PeLEDs and highlight the technological relevance of the approach. The
manuscript further benefits from a broad and well-integrated set of spectroscopic analyses (TRPL, TA, temperature-
dependent PL, Raman), providing multi-angle evidence for weakened EP interactions. Overall, the work represents a
significant and timely contribution to advancing perovskite NPL-based optoelectronics.
While this work has many merits, we believe that several fundamental issues require further clarification and supporting
evidence.
Regarding these points, I comment on points below.
<Lack of quantitative evaluation of AEBS incorporation>
Although FTIR and XPS analyses confirm AEBS adsorption, the manuscript does not offer quantitative information regarding
the extent of ligand exchange. The relative proportions of AEBS and native OLA ligands remain unclear.
To substantiate the mechanistic claims, quantitative measurements (e.g., TGA, quantitative NMR, or XPS ratio analysis)
should be provided to determine the ligand coverage and the AEBS/OLA ratio.

The use of SBA-15 as a slow-release matrix to mitigate structural degradation during AEBS treatment is intriguing, but its
generality remains ambiguous. It is unclear whether this approach applies to other highly polar or rigid ligands.

release-time dependence would greatly strengthen the methodological section.
<Insufficient discussion of broader electronic and interfacial effects>
Beyond EP coupling suppression, AEBS—owing to its strong polarity and rigid structure—may influence trap densities,
surface dipoles, and ion migration. UPS data suggest modifications to energy alignment, yet the manuscript does not fully
explore the broader electronic implications.
A more detailed analysis separating EP-related effects from defect passivation and ion-transport effects would provide a
more complete and accurate interpretation of the results.
<Limited insights into device degradation pathways>
While the reported operational stability is excellent, the manuscript provides little mechanistic insight into degradation
processes.
Analyses such as EL spectral evolution under bias, voltage rise during operation, or ion migration–related signatures would
help clarify the origin of the improved device lifetime and reinforce the claims of structural stabilization.
<Oversimplified attribution of emission broadening in the control NPLs>
The authors attribute the broader emission linewidth of the control sample primarily to enhanced EP coupling. However,
other factors, including trap-mediated recombination, surface reconstruction, and OLA desorption, are also likely
contributors, particularly in light of the stability data presented in the SI.
A more nuanced discussion acknowledging these additional mechanisms is recommended.
I think, the manuscript presents impactful results and a highly interesting mechanistic strategy. However, the issues raised
above, particularly regarding ligand quantification, method generalizability, and degradation analysis, must be satisfactorily
addressed to solidify the mechanistic claims and the robustness of the conclusions.

Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We agree that, in general, an
increased E is expected to enhance radiative recombination and shorten the PL lifetime
b
when exciton recombination dominates. However, in strongly quantum-confined NPL
systems, the recombination kinetics may be influenced by more complex factors.
In this system, the recombination dynamics are simultaneously regulated by EP
coupling through both radiative and non-radiative pathways. Based on PLQY and TRPL
analyses (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Table 2), AEBS treatment leads to a significant
reduction in the nonradiative rate (k ) from 0.0238 to 0.0115 ns-1, accompanied by an
nr
increase in the radiative rate (k ) from 0.0406 to 0.0426 ns-1. It should be emphasized
r
that in perovskites, defect trapping and exciton dissociation are typical phonon-assisted
processes, the rates of which are closely related to the EP coupling strength (Nano-
Micro Lett., 2024, 16, 178). Therefore, the weakening of EP coupling itself can
significantly inhibit phonon-assisted carrier trapping, thereby reducing non-radiative
recombination.
Furthermore, in strongly confined systems, the radiative recombination rate is not
solely determined by the electron-hole wavefunction overlap and may also be partially
influenced by phonon-mediated transfer between bright and dark exciton states (Nano
Lett., 2020, 20, 7321; Nano Lett., 2022, 17, 7011; Nat. Commun., 2023, 14, 2426; Adv.
Sci., 2022, 9, 2103013). Therefore, this may account for the lack of a significant
increase in the radiative recombination rate. The extended lifetime in AEBS-NPLs
primarily originates from the inhibition of phonon-assisted non-radiative processes due
to the weakened EP coupling, which is internally consistent with our proposed EP
coupling regulation mechanism. Notably, the coexistence of higher exciton binding
energy and extended PL lifetime in perovskites has been previously reported (Angew.
Chem. Int. Ed., 2024, 63, e202318777; Nat. Nanotechnol., 2025, 20, 507; Adv. Funct.
Mater., 2024, 2311554).

Q6. The manuscript states that both Joule heating and electric-field-induced
degradation are significantly suppressed. Could the authors elaborate on the mechanism
behind this suppression?
Reply:
Reduced Joule heating can be attributed to the mitigated EP coupling and
improved energy-level alignment. Weakened EP coupling enhances carrier mobility
and suppresses phonon-assisted trapping (Fig. 3a-f). Meanwhile, the improved energy-
level alignment reduces the hole-injection barrier and facilitates more balanced charge
injection (Fig. 3a,b and Supplementary Figs. 24,30). Together, these effects effectively
lower the device series resistance (Adv. Mater., 2024, 37, 2412041; Nat. Rev. Chem.,
2025, 9, 261; Nat. Commun., 2016, 7, 11755; ACS Energy Lett., 2017, 2, 1539; Nat.
Commun., 2023, 14, 6441), mitigate nonradiative recombination losses (ACS Nano
2016, 10, 9992; Nat. Photon., 2022, 16, 485; Adv. Mater., 2023, 35, 2209002; Nat.
Commun., 2020, 11, 2712; Nano Lett., 2018, 18, 6645; ACS Nano 2019, 13, 11433),
and consequently suppress Joule heating.
The suppression of electric-field-induced degradation is fundamentally linked to
the inhibition of halide ion migration and enhanced structural integrity. AEBS-NPLs
exhibit a significantly higher ion migration activation energy of 184 meV compared to
106 meV for Control-NPLs (Fig. R5), thereby hindering ion migration (Nat. Photon.,
2017, 11, 726; Nat. Energy, 2020, 5, 131; Nat. Nanotechnol., 2024, 19, 638).
Meanwhile, weakened EP coupling and improved energy-level alignment reduce series
resistance and nonradiative losses, thereby alleviating the impact of Joule heating on
ion migration (Supplementary Fig. 39; Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 6561). In addition,
the rigid vertical anchoring of AEBS ligands on the NPL surface constrains neighboring
ligand motion and lattice fluctuations (Fig. 1b), suppressing local structural
rearrangements and avoiding perovskite degradation under high electric fields.

Q7. Although improved injection efficiency may contribute to a reduced turn-on
voltage, it is unclear from Figure 4d what primarily accounts for the observed decrease
of 0.2-0.3 V. The authors should clarify this point.
Reply:
In response to the reviewer’s comment, we provide the following additional
clarification. The observed 0.2-0.3 V reduction in turn-on voltage can be ascribed to the
synergistic effects of balanced carrier injection, efficient transport, and reduced
nonradiative losses (Nature 2018, 562, 245; Sci. Adv., 2024, 10, eadp8473; Light Sci.
Appl., 2025, 14, 50). After AEBS post-treatment, the interfacial energy-level alignment
was optimized (Supplementary Fig. 30), thereby lowering the hole injection barrier
and enabling more balanced charge injection and radiative recombination at lower
voltages. In parallel, the rigid AEBS ligands pin surface OLA conformations, which
weakens EP coupling, reduces carrier-phonon scattering, and enhances carrier mobility
under low electric fields (Supplementary Table 1). Building on the improved injection
and transport, the suppressed EP coupling, together with the reduced defect density,
inhibits phonon-assisted trap capture and nonradiative recombination, thereby lowering
the carrier density threshold required for efficient radiative recombination. Collectively,
these effects account for the reduced turn-on voltage, consistent with the faster response
observed in Tr-EL measurements (Fig. 4h). We thank the reviewer for the comment
and have supplemented the manuscript accordingly.

Q2. The authors claim AEBS vertically pins on the CsPbI NPL surface. However, there

Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We agree that directly resolving
the precise orientation of organic ligands on NPL surfaces is important. However, due
to the limitations of current experimental techniques, the ligand geometry at the atomic
scale still cannot be unambiguously determined under realistic surface coverage
conditions. Consequently, ligand configurations on the nanocrystals are generally
inferred from density functional theory (DFT) calculations and further validated by
spectroscopic evidence (Fig. R8, Science 2024, 384, 189; Nature 2024, 631, 73; Nature
2023, 5, 830; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2025, e19659; Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 9211).
Following this established framework, our DFT calculations systematically compare
possible binding motifs of AEBS on the CsPbI NPL surface and identify the head-end
3
coordination configuration as the energetically most favorable (Supplementary Fig. 1).
This configuration involves simultaneous coordination between the sulfonyl group and
surface Pb2+ ions, as well as hydrogen bonding between −NH groups and surface I-
2
ions, which naturally leads to a preferentially upright orientation of the AEBS
backbone. XPS and FTIR analyses further support this assignment by confirming the
expected coordination environment and hydrogen-bonding interactions at the NPL-
ligand interface (Supplementary Fig. 12).

this mechanism is not inferred from theory alone. Molecular dynamics calculations
show a clear reduction in temporal fluctuations of the distances between terminal
carbon atoms of adjacent OLA ligands after AEBS incorporation (Supplementary Fig.
2). Experimentally, FTIR spectroscopy provides a sensitive probe of alkyl-chain
conformational order (Fig. R9, Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 9211; J. Am. Chem. Soc.,
2020, 142, 13051; J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1999, 121, 5319; Molecules 2020, 25, 5633; J.
Am. Chem. Soc., 1987, 109, 3559). Upon AEBS treatment, the ν (CH )/ν (CH )
as 2 s 2

narrowing of both vibrational bands (Fig. 1e). These spectral changes are well-
established signatures of enhanced alkyl chain order and suppressed conformational
dynamics of OLA ligands.

Q3. How can the authors rule out that the observed effects are not simply due to superior
surface passivation by AEBS, rather than the proposed "pinning" of OLA ligands? The
study lacks a control experiment using a structurally similar but flexible ligand to isolate
the effect of ligand rigidity from other chemical properties.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment on distinguishing surface defect
passivation from rigid-ligand pinning. To decouple these two effects, we designed
systematic control experiments using oleylammonium iodide (OLAI) and 3-Amino-1-
propanesulfonamide (APSA). OLAI treatment increases the surface coverage of OLA
and effectively passivates surface defects without introducing new ligand species (Fig.
R10a,b). In contrast, APSA shares the same head and tail functional groups as AEBS
but lacks a rigid aromatic backbone, serving as a flexible analogue to isolate the role of
ligand rigidity (Fig. R10c,d). As shown in Fig. R11, both OLAI-NPLs and APSA-NPLs
exhibit higher PLQYs than Control-NPLs, confirming effective defect passivation.
However, their PL linewidths remain largely unchanged, indicating that defect
passivation alone does not lead to emission narrowing. FTIR analysis further reveals
that both increasing OLA coverage and introducing a flexible APSA ligand fail to
restrict the conformational freedom of the alkyl chains (Fig. R12 and Fig. 1e).
Temperature-dependent PL linewidth fitting shows that Γ slightly increases for
LO
OLAI-NPLs compared to Control-NPLs due to the higher density of long-chain OLA,
whereas Γ for APSA-NPLs shows only a minor reduction compared to Control-NPLs
LO
and remains significantly larger than that of AEBS-NPLs (Fig. R13 and Fig. 2i). These
results demonstrate that flexible ligands or increased surface passivation alone cannot
effectively suppress EP coupling, and that rigid AEBS ligand pinning plays a dominant
role in doing so.

Q4. The reported maximum EQE of 29.8% is an outlier in the statistical distribution
(19.3% to 29.8%), and the average EQE is 23.2 ± 2.4%. The large standard deviation
suggests significant device-to-device variation, raising a concern about the
reproducibility and the representativeness of the champion device.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for the careful examination of the EQE statistics and
device-to-device variation. The reported EQE statistics are compiled from devices
independently fabricated across multiple batches over an extended period, rather than
from a single optimized experiment. It is important to note that perovskite
optoelectronic properties are intrinsically sensitive to surface states and processing
conditions. In addition, in our system, precise control of the AEBS/SBA-15 ligand post-
treatment process remains challenging. These factors inevitably introduce batch-to-
batch variability under practical fabrication conditions and thereby induce performance
variation. Despite this variability, the devices exhibit an average EQE of 23.2±2.4%,
with all devices outperforming the best Control-NPLs based PeLEDs. The maximum
EQE of 29.8% lies within the continuous tail of the statistical distribution rather than
representing an isolated outlier, with a substantial fraction of devices exceeding 25%.
Similar EQE statistical distributions have also been widely reported in many previously
reported high-performance LEDs (Fig. R14, Nat. Commun., 2019, 10, 3624; Nat.
Photon., 2025, 19, 952; Nat. Commun., 2023, 14, 397; Nature 2021, 591, 72),
supporting the representativeness and reproducibility of the results.

Q5. The improved device performance is primarily attributed to suppressed EP coupling.
However, other factors—such as enhanced surface passivation, improved energy level
alignment, or reduced defect density—could also or more significantly contribute to
these improvements. How can the authors deconvolve the contribution of suppressed
EP coupling from other beneficial effects of AEBS treatment?
Reply:
We appreciate the reviewer’s professional suggestion to deconvolve the multiple
physical factors influenced by AEBS. To rigorously isolate the specific contribution of
EP coupling suppression, we designed a systematic comparative study: (1) defect-
passivated NPLs using OLAI without introducing new ligand species (OLAI-NPLs);
(2) NPLs treated with APSA (APSA-NPLs) which shares same head and tail functional
groups as AEBS but lacks a rigid backbone (Fig. R10).
OLAI-NPLs exhibit effective defect passivation (Fig. R11b). However, FTIR
analysis shows that the increased surface coverage of OLA ligands enhances
conformational disorder (Fig. R12) and the resulting EP coupling (Fig. R13c).
Moreover, OLAI-NPLs show no significant narrowing of the emission linewidth, nor
do they exhibit improvements in electrical conductivity or device EQE relative to the
control samples (Figs. R11a, R15a, and R16a). These results demonstrate that defect
passivation alone cannot account for the substantial performance enhancement
observed for AEBS-modified devices.
APSA possesses the same head and tail functional groups as AEBS but lacks a
rigid backbone. Unlike AEBS, the APSA fails to effectively suppress the
conformational freedom of the alkyl chains, do not significantly reduce the EP coupling
strength, and also do not exhibit substantial improvements in electrical conductivity or
device EQE (Figs. R12, R13d, R15b and R16b). These findings effectively rule out the
possibility that other chemical contributions of AEBS, such as its short-chain nature
and defect passivation by the functional groups, are the primary drivers of the observed
substantial performance improvement.
In contrast, only the rigid AEBS treatment achieves substantial EP coupling
suppression, which we identify as the dominant mechanism for suppressing exciton
dissociation, reducing carrier-phonon scattering, and achieving narrow emission and
enhanced mobility. In addition, AEBS pinning suppresses lattice vibrations and local
structural rearrangements (Fig. 1b), enhancing lattice stability. EP coupling suppression
further promotes efficient charge transport and reduces nonradiative recombination,
which lowers Joule heating (Supplementary Fig. 39), mitigates ion migration, and
enhances device stability.
Although AEBS modification optimizes energy-level alignment, promotes
balanced charge injection, and lowers the turn-on voltage (Fig.4d), the simultaneous
improvements in device efficiency, operational stability, and emission linewidth
correlate more strongly with the pronounced enhancements in the intrinsic optical
properties, electrical conductivity, and stability of the AEBS-NPLs. Energy-level
alignment alone is insufficient to account for such a substantial and concerted
enhancement, indicating that it is not the primary driving factor for the improved device
performance. Instead, the effective suppression of EP coupling plays a dominant role
and, in synergy with energy-level optimization and defect passivation, endows the
devices with superior optoelectronic performance.

(Supplementary Figs. 25 and 37), and the manuscript has been correspondingly
expanded.
